units.text: In a few cases, the GNU utilities’ default behavior is incompatible with the POSIX standard. To suppress these incompatibilities, define the ⟦0⟧ environment variable. Unless you are checking for POSIX conformance, you probably do not need to define ⟦1⟧.
units.sourceHTML: In a few cases, the GNU utilities’ default behavior is incompatible with the POSIX standard. To suppress these incompatibilities, define the POSIXLY_CORRECT environment variable. Unless you are checking for POSIX conformance, you probably do not need to define POSIXLY_CORRECT.

units.text: Normally options and operands can appear in any order, and programs act as if all the options appear before any operands. For example, ‘⟦0⟧’ acts like ‘⟦1⟧’, since ‘⟦2⟧’ is an option-argument of ⟦3⟧. However, if the ⟦4⟧ environment variable is set, options must appear before operands, unless otherwise specified for a particular command.
units.sourceHTML: Normally options and operands can appear in any order, and programs act as if all the options appear before any operands. For example, ‘diff lao tzu -C 2’ acts like ‘diff -C 2 lao tzu’, since ‘2’ is an option-argument of -C. However, if the POSIXLY_CORRECT environment variable is set, options must appear before operands, unless otherwise specified for a particular command.

units.text: Newer versions of POSIX are occasionally incompatible with older versions. For example, older versions of POSIX allowed the command ‘⟦0⟧’ to have the same meaning as ‘⟦1⟧’, but POSIX 1003.1-2001 ‘⟦2⟧’ no longer allows digit-string options like ⟦3⟧.
units.sourceHTML: Newer versions of POSIX are occasionally incompatible with older versions. For example, older versions of POSIX allowed the command ‘diff -c -10’ to have the same meaning as ‘diff -C 10’, but POSIX 1003.1-2001 ‘diff’ no longer allows digit-string options like -10.

units.text: The GNU utilities normally conform to the version of POSIX that is standard for your system. To cause them to conform to a different version of POSIX, define the ⟦0⟧ environment variable to a value of the form ⟦1⟧ specifying the year and month the standard was adopted. Two values are currently supported for ⟦2⟧: ‘⟦3⟧’ stands for POSIX 1003.2-1992, and ‘⟦4⟧’ stands for POSIX 1003.1-2001. For example, if you are running older software that assumes an older version of POSIX and uses ‘⟦5⟧’, you can work around the compatibility problems by setting ‘⟦6⟧’ in your environment.
units.sourceHTML: The GNU utilities normally conform to the version of POSIX that is standard for your system. To cause them to conform to a different version of POSIX, define the _POSIX2_VERSION environment variable to a value of the form yyyymm specifying the year and month the standard was adopted. Two values are currently supported for _POSIX2_VERSION: ‘199209’ stands for POSIX 1003.2-1992, and ‘200112’ stands for POSIX 1003.1-2001. For example, if you are running older software that assumes an older version of POSIX and uses ‘diff -c -10’, you can work around the compatibility problems by setting ‘_POSIX2_VERSION=199209’ in your environment.
